analysis.one_liner: Cracks down on offshore tax havens, hedge fund secrecy, and tax shelter promoters.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the Senate on July 12, 2011 with seven cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Finance Committee and never received a committee vote or floor vote before the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have given the Treasury new power to restrict banks and countries that block U.S. tax enforcement, treated foreign corporations actually managed from the United States as domestic companies for tax purposes, and presumed that money moving through banks that refuse the new foreign-account reporting rules is unreported income. It also required multinational companies to report employees, sales, and taxes paid country by country, imposed anti-money-laundering duties on hedge funds and company formation agents, taxed offshore credit-default-swap payments as U.S. income, and raised penalties for advisers who promote tax shelters or collect fees tied to tax savings. The bill never advanced past its referral to the Finance Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who bear more of the tax burden when wealthy individuals and multinational companies move income offshore or use shelters to understate what they owe. Also honest businesses competing against rivals whose profits are booked in tax havens.

how_it_helps.text: Treats foreign corporations managed and controlled primarily in the United States as domestic corporations for income tax purposes, closing the structure used to book profits offshore while the decisions are made here.

Creates a rebuttable presumption that a U.S. person who formed, funded, or benefited from an offshore entity holding accounts at a foreign bank that does not comply with FATCA reporting controls that entity, and that money received through it is taxable income, shifting the burden of proof to the taxpayer.

Requires SEC-registered corporations to report employees, sales, financing, tax obligations, and tax payments on a country-by-country basis, making it visible when profits are booked in low-tax jurisdictions where little business is done.
Treats credit default swap payments sent to offshore recipients as U.S.-source income subject to tax.

Raises penalties to up to 150% of gross income for promoting abusive tax shelters or aiding understatement of tax liability, makes those penalties non-deductible, and bans tax advisers' contingent-fee agreements based on projected tax savings.

Requires unregistered investment companies such as hedge funds and private equity funds, and companies in the business of forming new legal entities, to run anti-money-laundering programs and file suspicious activity reports.
Authorizes the Treasury to restrict correspondent accounts and payment cards of foreign jurisdictions or institutions that impede U.S. tax enforcement or raise money laundering concerns.

analysis.who_pays: Wealthy individuals using offshore accounts and entities, multinational corporations shifting profits into tax havens, hedge funds and private equity funds facing new reporting and anti-money-laundering duties, offshore banks that refuse to share account information, and tax advisers and law firms who earn fees from shelter promotion.
analysis.who_pays_short: Wealthy offshore users, banks, tax advisers

drawbacks.text: The presumption rules could sweep in legitimate transactions: a business or family trust banking with a non-compliant foreign institution would have to rebut a presumption of control or unreported income with clear and convincing evidence, raising litigation and compliance costs even for people not evading taxes.

Compliance costs fall heavily on financial institutions, fund managers, and multinationals, which would bear new reporting, examination, and anti-money-laundering obligations; opponents of such measures have long argued those costs are passed to customers and investors.

Reaching into foreign banks and jurisdictions risks friction with other countries' banking systems and legal regimes, since the Treasury could cut off correspondent accounts and card networks of institutions it deems to be impeding tax enforcement.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core goal — making it harder and costlier to hide money offshore or sell tax shelters — would recover revenue and shift tax burden back toward those best able to pay, which most honestly benefits everyone else. The real cost is blunt instrument risk: presumption rules and cutoff powers aimed at secrecy jurisdictions can entangle legitimate cross-border banking and business, and multinationals face heavy new disclosure duties. The tradeoff favors ordinary taxpayers, but the design would need careful regulatory line-drawing to avoid penalizing ordinary account holders at banks that simply refuse to comply with FATCA.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it — no markup, no vote — before the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Sen. Carl Levin introduced the Stop Tax Haven Abuse Act on July 12, 2011, joined by seven cosponsors (six Democrats and one Independent).
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, the only formal action ever taken on the bill.
The bill died in the Finance Committee without a hearing, markup, or vote, and never reached the Senate floor before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wealthy individuals and multinational companies using offshore structures kept the status quo, along with the offshore banks, hedge funds, and tax advisers whose business depends on it; ordinary taxpayers continued to cover the revenue lost to evasion.

for.name: Sen. Carl Levin
for.role: U.S. Senator from Michigan; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Stop Tax Haven Abuse Act and delivered introductory remarks on it in the Senate.

for.name: 7 Senate cosponsors
for.role: Cosponsors, including Sens. Conrad, Nelson of Florida, Shaheen, Whitehouse, and others
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (6 Democrats and 1 Independent, Sen. Sanders).

against.name: Senate Finance Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup; the bill sat in committee for the rest of the Congress and died without any committee action.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat or Independent; no Republican signed on, and the Democratic-run Finance Committee never brought the bill to a vote, so it never faced a recorded party split on the floor.

industries.industry: Offshore banks and tax haven financial institutions
industries.note: The bill lets Treasury cut off correspondent accounts and card access of jurisdictions and institutions that impede U.S. tax enforcement, and presumes money moved through non-FATCA banks is unreported income. These banks' business model depends on secrecy the bill is designed to pierce.

Country-by-country reporting would expose where profits, employees, and tax payments actually sit, and the managed-and-controlled rule would tax foreign corporations run from the U.S. as domestic companies, shrinking the value of haven booking.

industries.industry: Hedge funds and private equity funds
industries.note: The bill sets a deadline for anti-money-laundering programs and suspicious activity reporting for unregistered investment funds, ending a gap in which they operated without those obligations.

industries.industry: Tax advisers, law firms, and accounting firms
industries.note: Penalties for promoting shelters rise to 150% of gross income and become non-deductible, and contingent-fee arrangements tied to projected tax savings are banned, directly cutting into shelter-promotion revenue.

Firms that create corporations, LLCs, and trusts for clients would be brought under the Bank Secrecy Act with anti-money-laundering duties, closing the loophole that made anonymous shell companies easy to buy.

industries.industry: Honest domestic businesses and wage-earning taxpayers
industries.note: Curbing offshore evasion and shelters narrows the gap between what compliant taxpayers pay and what evaders avoid, easing the shifted burden on people and businesses that play by the rules.
